tone_statements.citation: Rogers, Christopher (2011). A comparative grammar of Xinkan. University of Utah.
tone_statements.quote: Xinkan languages, unlike some other languages in the Mesoamerican linguistic area, do not have tonal contrasts, and similar to other languages in the linguistic area, stress placement is predictable. Stress assignment in Xinkan languages is simple and straightforward: the stressed syllable, or more accurately the stress bearing vowel, is always the last vowel before the rightmost consonant. This is represented in (117). (117) Xinkan stress placement V -> V́ / __C(V)# [...] The words in (118) are taken from the Chiquimulilla lexicon, though the stress patterns are applicable to all of the Xinkan languages. [...] In most words, those that end in a V, stress is placed on the penultimate syllable. However, if a grammatical morpheme of the shape /-C(V)/ is added to a word the stress shifts to right before this suffix, as in t'uúri 'bird' and t'uurí-n' 'my bird' in (118), as predicted by the rule that stress falls on the last vowel before the last consonant of a word.

tone_statements.summary: Matches the catalog entry point for point: no tone; stress on the last vowel before the rightmost consonant (V -> stressed / __C(V)#), i.e. penultimate in V-final words, final in C-final words; a -C(V) suffix pulls stress rightward (t'uúri vs t'uurí-n'). Secondary stress is not mentioned. Vowel length is not stated as a factor; the t'uúri/t'uurí-n' pair shows a long vowel yielding stress to a shor

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator (Rogers 2010 sec. 3.5, printed pp. 134-136 = pp. 154-156). The deciding source is the only modern description of Jumaytepeque Xinka and the only descriptive reference Glottolog lists; it is a full comparative reference grammar by the fieldworker of record. The classification (weight-sensitive right-edge: final stress iff the word ends in a consonant, else penult; CVC heavy, long vowels not attracting stress, per t'uúri vs t'uurí-n') is a faithful reading of rule (117). An independent held source (Sachse 2010:216, citing Campbell 1972:187 and Schumann 1967:32) states the identical rule for Guazacapan Xinka with matching suffix-shift data. The only caveats are (a) Rogers illustrates with Chiquimulilla, asserting rather than exemplifying the Jumaytepeque case, and (b) the citable version of record is the paywalled 2016 UT Press book; neither is like

sources.note: Matches the catalog entry point for point: no tone; stress on the last vowel before the rightmost consonant (V -> stressed / __C(V)#), i.e. penultimate in V-final words, final in C-final words; a -C(V) suffix pulls stress rightward (t'uúri vs t'uurí-n'). sources.quote: 'In Xinka stress is phonologically conditioned and lies on the vowel preceding the last consonant in the word (i.e. V -> V́ / _C(V) #) (Campbell 1972a:187; 1997:166; see also Schumann 1967:32).' Semi-speaker data: [púla] 'to make', [pulá-ka] 'you made', [pula-ka-káŋ]; 'Stress shift is morphophonemic.' Data are colonial and modern Guazacapan Xinka, not Jumaytepeque.
